Public data case study · UCI Online Retail

One entry drove December’s cancellation spike

I looked at invoices from a UK online retailer to see what was behind the jump in recorded cancellations.

Explore by month

December 2011 is a partial month. Sales and cancellations are grouped by the month each invoice was recorded. A product’s cancellations can relate to purchases from a different month. Fees, postage and manual entries are shown on one separate line and left out of the product ranking.

ProductGross salesCancellation valueShare of month

What changes when we set both entries aside?

Set both entries aside and December’s recorded cancellations drop below November’s. The data covers only part of December, so these totals tell us how much was recorded in each period. To compare how often cancellations happened, we’d need a separate check.

The two invoice entries

InvoiceStock codeQuantityUnit priceSigned line value

The amounts are equal and the quantities have opposite signs. The records leave open whether the entries are linked and why the cancellation happened.

How I checked the numbers

Each input line falls into one category. Signed value is quantity multiplied by unit price. The dashboard reports cancellation value as a positive magnitude.

RuleSource rowsSigned value

SQL and pandas gave the same monthly totals from the prepared data. I also checked those totals directly against the original workbook. The Excel file shows the SQL and pandas figures side by side.

What I’d do next

If the team confirms a reversal, I’d show its impact separately in the monthly report. I’d then compare cancellation rates over equivalent periods before deciding whether there’s a wider problem.
